title: Thumbnail-Sized Bird Figurines Carved 40,000 Years Ago Unearthed in German Cave
summary: In the dim recesses of Germany's Hohle Fels cave, archaeologists have uncovered two tiny treasures that speak volumes about our ancient ancestors. The newly discovered bird figurines, carved from mammoth ivory, are roughly the size of a thumbnail—yet they're packed with exquisite detail, from the spread of a wing to the posture of a brooding bird. Dating back 40,000 years to the Aurignacian period, these miniature masterpieces add to a growing body of evidence that early Homo sapiens in Europe possessed a sophisticated artistic sensibility. "The figurines demonstrate that the earliest artists were skilled ivory-carvers, who could depict delicate motifs in miniature form," said Nicholas Conard, the University of Tübingen archaeologist who directs excavations at the site. The two carvings were found in 2025, lying just five feet apart in a layer that dates to the dawn of modern human presence in Europe, shortly after Neanderthals vanished. One bird appears to be lying on the ground, possibly brooding over its eggs—a position that suggests it's a ptarmigan, a game bird whose bones have been found in the same prehistoric layers. The second bird has spread wings, evoking either flight or a courtship display; it may also be a ptarmigan or perhaps a bird of prey. These figurines join a third water bird carving discovered at Hohle Fels in 2001, making the cave unique among Ice Age sites for its avian art. The cave—its name means "hollow rock"—is already renowned for the Venus of Hohle Fels, a 41,000-year-old female figurine considered Europe's oldest figurative sculpture. The new birds are significantly smaller than previous finds, yet Conard notes they are "not highly stylized but instead include many specific and unique features." The artist captured detailed observations that allow researchers to ponder the birds' species and behaviors. Why did Aurignacian people carve these tiny talismans? Archaeologists can only speculate. They may have served as personal amulets or group symbols. The prevalence of bird imagery at Hohle Fels reflects a deep connection to the natural world. As Stefanie Kölbl of the Museum of Prehistory and Ice Age Art put it, birds' calls signaled warnings, and their hollow bones were used to make flutes that produced "magical sounds." The figurines are on display at the museum in Blaubeuren through April 2027. To gaze upon them is to glimpse the mind of an artist who lived 400 centuries ago—someone who saw a bird, picked up a piece of ivory, and captured a moment of flight or tenderness in the palm of their hand.
why_it_matters: These carvings are a tiny piece of the big story of what makes us human—the urge to make art and give meaning to the world. By studying such finds, we learn that complex symbolic thinking appeared early in our species, long before writing or cities, and that creativity has always been part of our survival toolkit.

background_read: Hohle Fels cave (a site in southwestern Germany) is in a region called the Swabian Jura, where many of the world’s oldest musical instruments and figurines have been found. All come from the Aurignacian culture, the first Homo sapiens to spread across Europe.

Shortly before these figurines were carved, the last Neanderthals disappeared from the area. While Neanderthals made tools, there is little evidence they created representational art; the burst of human creativity on display here marks a major cognitive shift.

Mammoth ivory was a prized material for Ice Age artists. The carvings show that these people observed wildlife keenly—enough to make tiny sculptures recognizable to modern scientists as specific bird species.
The cave also contained early flutes made from bird bones and mammoth ivory, suggesting that music and symbolic art were already intertwined in daily life 40,000 years ago.

perspectives.description: The figurines show that even 40,000 years ago, humans were not just surviving—they were keen observers of animals and skilled artists. This discovery adds to the picture of a rich inner life among early modern humans right as they replaced Neanderthals in Europe.

Some researchers caution that we may read too much onto these objects; without written records, calling them ‘talismans’ or ‘art’ might reflect modern bias. It’s possible the carvings had mundane uses we haven’t guessed.

The find fits a broader pattern of symbolic artifacts appearing during the Aurignacian period across Europe, often in caves used repeatedly over generations. This suggests that shared beliefs and artistic traditions were already spreading among small, mobile hunter-gatherer groups.

Future digs at Hohle Fels and elsewhere may uncover even older examples of figurative art. If the timeline of human creativity keeps getting pushed back, our understanding of when and how language, music, and spirituality first appeared in our species might need to be rewritten.
